l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: After seven years of wandering, Aeneas and the Trojan fleet are driven toward Italy by a storm raised by Aeolus at Juno’s request. Neptune calms the sea, and Aeneas reaches a secure Libyan harbor with six other ships, where the Trojans hunt, feast, and mourn their scattered companions. Venus appeals to Jupiter, who confirms that Aeneas will found the Trojan line in Italy and that his descendants will lead to Rome’s greatness. Jupiter sends Mercury to ensure that the Trojans receive a friendly welcome in Carthage, where Queen Dido is expected to encounter Aeneas.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Aeneas leads the Trojans toward Italy after years of wandering, but Juno’s storm scatters and damages his fleet. He reaches the Libyan shore with six ships, hunts seven stags for his men, encourages them to endure, and mourns the absent Orontes, Gyas, Lycus, and Amycus. Jupiter declares that Aeneas will wage successful war in Italy, build cities, and eventually be taken up to heaven.

l: Juno, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Juno hates the Trojan race because of the judgment of Paris, Ganymede, Electra, and the injury to her marriage, and because she fears that the Trojans will destroy Carthage. She asks Aeolus to unleash the winds against Aeneas and his fleet.

l: Venus, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Venus sees Jupiter surveying the Libyan lands and appeals to him over Aeneas’s sufferings and the Trojans’ failure to reach Italy. Jupiter reassures her that fate still guarantees the Trojan future.

l: Jupiter, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Jupiter comforts Venus and confirms that Aeneas will reach Italy, defeat its nations, and establish cities. He outlines the succession from Ascanius and Alba Longa to Romulus and Rome, and sends Mercury to secure a friendly reception for the Trojans in Carthage.

l: Neptune, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Neptune sees the Trojan fleet scattered by the storm and rebukes the winds for disturbing his sea without his command. He calms the waters, clears the darkness, frees the ships from the shoals, and guides the surviving fleet toward land.

l: Aeolus, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Aeolus rules the imprisoned winds from a cavern and can release or restrain them. At Juno’s request, he unleashes the winds against the Trojan fleet in return for Deiopeia as his wife.

l: Dido, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Dido is identified in the argument as the queen of Carthage. Venus’s device causes her to begin developing a passion for Aeneas, and she asks him to recount his adventures after the siege of Troy.

l: the Trojans, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: The Trojans have wandered for seven years after leaving Troy and are scattered by Juno’s storm. The survivors reach the Libyan shore, recover from the sea, hunt and prepare food, and fear for companions who have not arrived. Jupiter ensures that they will receive protection in Carthage.

l: Carthage, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Carthage is an ancient Tyrian colony on the African coast, prosperous in war and trade and especially beloved by Juno. Juno fears that the future Trojan race will destroy its towers, while Jupiter orders Mercury to open its ports to Trojan guests.

l: Italy, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Italy is the land toward which Aeneas and the Trojans are sailing. Jupiter declares that Aeneas will wage successful war there, impose laws, build cities, and establish the Trojan succession.

l: Latium, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Latium is the realm destined for Aeneas and his descendants. Jupiter promises that Aeneas will reach its promised throne and that Ascanius will later transfer the seat from Lavinium to Alba Longa.

l: Rome, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Rome is presented as the future city founded by Romulus, descendant of the Trojan line. Jupiter says that Rome will rule the world, impose laws, and receive lasting glory.

l: Troy, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Troy has been ruined in war, and its surviving people have been driven into exile. Jupiter foretells that Troy’s descendants will later overturn the Grecian state and take revenge on those who caused its fall.

l: Libya, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Libya is the region where Jupiter observes human misery and where the surviving Trojan ships find refuge. The Trojans reach a sheltered harbor on its coast after Neptune calms the sea.

l: the storm, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: The storm is raised by Aeolus at Juno’s request and scatters the Trojan fleet across the sea. It sinks or damages ships, kills or separates crew members, and is finally calmed by Neptune.

l: Aeneas’s voyage, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: The Trojan voyage has lasted seven years after the departure from Troy and has carried the exiles through repeated dangers. The fleet is now sailing toward Italy when Juno’s storm forces the surviving ships to the Libyan coast.

l: the Trojan War, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: The Trojan War destroyed Troy and left Aeneas and the surviving Trojans exiled. Juno recalls having fought the Trojans on behalf of conquering Greece, while Jupiter foretells that their descendants will later defeat the Grecian state.

l: the founding of Rome, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: The founding of Rome is traced through Aeneas, Ascanius, Alba Longa, Ilia, and Romulus. Romulus is destined to gain his grandsire’s throne, found the city, and give the Roman people their name.

l: Fate, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: Fate fixes the Trojans’ future despite Juno’s hostility and their present sufferings. It guarantees Aeneas’s arrival in Italy, the succession through Ascanius and Alba Longa, the rise of Romulus, and the unbounded empire of Rome.

l: Roman imperial rule, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: The Roman empire is foretold to rule the subject world without assigned bounds or a term of years. Jupiter says that Caesar from the Julian stock will rise, with an empire bounded only by the ocean and a fame bounded only by the skies.

l: Trojan fleet, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: The Trojan fleet leaves the Sicilian shores but is attacked by winds raised by Aeolus. One ship is overwhelmed, several are driven onto rocks or sand, and seven ships eventually reach a secure harbor on the Libyan coast.

l: the ships, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: The ships are battered by waves, torn sails, broken cables, and rushing seawater. Several are wrecked or stranded, while seven surviving ships enter the sheltered harbor and are later freed from the shoals by Neptune.

l: the Roman succession, The Aeneid, BOOK I
s: The Roman succession is foretold from Aeneas to Ascanius, who will reign for thirty years and build Alba Longa after moving the seat from Lavinium. After three hundred years, Ilia will bear Romulus and Remus, and Romulus will establish Rome.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, Meantime, in shades of night Aeneas lies:
s: Aeneas explores the unfamiliar Libyan coast after a sleepless night and encounters Venus disguised as a huntress. Venus tells him that he is near Carthage, a Tyrian colony ruled by Dido, and recounts how Dido fled Tyre after her brother Pygmalion murdered her husband, Sichaeus. Dido and her companions seized a fleet, carried away Pygmalion’s treasure, and founded the new settlement after landing in Libya. Venus then asks Aeneas about his origins and his purpose in the region.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, Meantime, in shades of night Aeneas lies:
s: Aeneas surveys the unknown coast after his fleet takes shelter beneath rocks. He encounters Venus disguised as a huntress and asks what land he has reached and who rules it.

l: Venus, The Aeneid, Meantime, in shades of night Aeneas lies:
s: Venus appears to Aeneas in the forest disguised as a huntress and initially claims to be a Tyrian virgin. She identifies the region as Libya and tells Aeneas about Dido, Carthage, and Dido’s flight from Tyre.

l: Dido, The Aeneid, Meantime, in shades of night Aeneas lies:
s: Dido rules the growing city of Carthage after fleeing Tyre because of her brother Pygmalion’s hostility. She had been married to Sichaeus, whose murder was revealed to her by his ghost, and she led companions away with a fleet and his hidden treasure.

l: Carthage, The Aeneid, Meantime, in shades of night Aeneas lies:
s: Carthage is a rising city in Libya and a Tyrian colony ruled by Dido. Its turrets can be seen from the coast where Aeneas arrives.

l: Dido's flight from Tyre, The Aeneid, Meantime, in shades of night Aeneas lies:
s: After Sichaeus’s ghost reveals that Pygmalion murdered him for his wealth, Dido gathers companions who hate or fear the tyrant. They seize ready ships, take Pygmalion’s treasure, and sail from Tyre to Libya.

l: the founding of Carthage, The Aeneid, Meantime, in shades of night Aeneas lies:
s: Dido and her companions land in Libya and purchase a piece of ground called Byrsa. They enclose and wall the area using a bull’s hide, establishing the site of new Carthage.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Aeneas and his surviving companions reach the Libyan coast after storms scatter the Trojan fleet. Venus guides Aeneas and Achates, concealed by clouds, into Dido’s rising city, where they see paintings of the Trojan War and find the missing Trojans pleading for refuge. Dido welcomes Aeneas, promises aid, and holds a feast, while Venus sends Cupid in Ascanius’s form to inspire Dido with an irresistible love. Venus hides the real Ascanius in a magical sleep while Cupid prepares to carry out the deception.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Aeneas tells Venus, while she is disguised as a nymph, that he was driven from ancient Troy and has been tossed across many seas before reaching the Libyan coast. He enters Dido’s city concealed by Venus’s clouds, recognizes the Trojan paintings, and is reunited with his companions when Dido grants the Trojans refuge. Aeneas presents himself to Dido, thanks her for her kindness, embraces his friends, and attends the feast prepared for him.

l: Venus, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Venus appears to Aeneas in borrowed form, directs him toward Dido’s city, and conceals him and Achates in clouds. She later reveals herself, leaves for Paphos, and then devises a plan to protect Aeneas by sending Cupid in Ascanius’s shape to make Dido fall in love with him. Venus puts the real Ascanius into a gentle sleep and carries him to her groves.

l: Dido, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Dido rules the rising Tyrian city, hears petitions, dispenses laws, and directs its building. She welcomes the shipwrecked Trojans, promises to repair their fleet and provide protection, and recognizes Aeneas as the son of Venus and Anchises. She leads Aeneas to her palace and hosts a splendid feast, while Venus plans to make her fall violently in love.

l: Cupid, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Cupid obeys Venus’s command to assume the shape and face of Ascanius. He is to bring Aeneas’s gifts to Dido and infuse her with a love so strong that neither age nor art can cure it.

l: Ascanius, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Ascanius is the boy whom Aeneas sends for from the ships with precious gifts for Dido. Venus places him in a pleasing sleep, carries him away to her blissful groves, and substitutes Cupid in his form.

l: Juno, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Juno is associated with the Tyrian city, which Dido’s people regard as under her care. Venus fears Juno’s influence and suspects that the city may endanger Aeneas’s interests.

l: the Trojans, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: The Trojans are survivors driven from Troy and scattered by storms. Their representatives appeal to Dido for shelter, repairs for their ships, and permission to continue toward Italy or return to Acestes; Dido grants their requests and welcomes them.

l: Tyrians, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: The Tyrians are building Dido’s new city by raising walls and a citadel, laying foundations, making laws, and preparing a theatre. They are compared to bees laboring together, and they pity and receive the shipwrecked Trojans.

l: Troy, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Troy is the ancient city from which Aeneas and the Trojans were expelled by force. Its destruction and suffering are represented in paintings on the walls of Dido’s temple.

l: Carthage, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Carthage is identified through Dido’s reference to the Carthaginian coasts, which she hopes the storm will bring Aeneas’s wandering king to.

l: Libya, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: The Trojans land on the Libyan coast after being tossed by storms. Aeneas wanders alone in the Libyan deserts before Venus guides him toward Dido’s city.

l: Italy, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Italy is the fruitful region toward which Aeneas and the Trojans originally direct their voyage. Ilioneus says they still intend to pursue Italy if their ships can be repaired.

l: Trojan fleet, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: The Trojan fleet is reduced from twice ten ships to seven after storms. Venus predicts that the scattered ships and their crews have reached the harbor or are approaching, and Dido offers timber, repairs, and ships of convoy.

l: the Trojan War, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: The Trojan War is depicted in Dido’s temple, including the Greeks’ assault, the Trojans’ defeats, Achilles’s pursuit of the Trojans, the deaths of Rhesus, Troilus, and Hector, Priam’s suffering, and the fighting of Memnon and Penthesilea.

l: Aeneas’s voyage, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Aeneas’s voyage begins after the Trojans are expelled from Troy and is marked by varied seas, storms, and the loss or scattering of ships. Its intended destination is Italy, but the surviving fleet is driven to the Libyan coast.

l: shipwreck, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: The Trojans suffer shipwreck and fear being driven from Dido’s shore back into the cruel seas. Ilioneus asks Dido to spare the survivors, and she promises that the men will be received and the fleet repaired.

l: the Trojan paintings, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: The Trojan paintings cover the walls of Dido’s temple and show events and leaders from the Trojan War. Aeneas recognizes scenes of Troy’s suffering and is moved to tears while studying them.

l: Venus’s love potion, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Venus’s love potion is described as a gentle poison or venom that Cupid will infuse into Dido’s veins. Its purpose is to create a violent and lasting love for Aeneas.

l: the feast, The Aeneid, To whom, with sorrow streaming from his eyes,
s: Dido prepares a feast for Aeneas and the Trojans, with incense, rich foods, wine, purple hangings, Tyrian carpets, and costly vessels. Aeneas sends Ascanius with precious gifts intended for the queen during the feast.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: Cupid assumes the form and face of Aeneas and follows Achates to the feast, where he presents gifts and secretly kindles Dido's love for Aeneas. Dido hosts the Trojan and Tyrian guests with food, wine, prayers, music, and conversation. During the feast, Iopas sings of the heavens and nature, while Dido questions Aeneas about Priam, Hector, the Trojan War, and his flight and wanderings. She finally asks him to recount the Grecian stratagems, the fall of the town, and the hardships he endured.

l: Cupid, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: Cupid assumes the form and face of Aeneas, follows Achates at a shorter pace, and brings the gifts. He plays with Aeneas's children and embraces them before approaching Dido, whom he secretly causes to abandon her former care and love Aeneas.

l: Dido, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: Dido hosts the Trojan and Tyrian guests and presides over the feast. She is captivated by Cupid in Aeneas's form, drinks deeply of love for Aeneas, asks many questions about Troy and its heroes, and requests the full story of the war and Aeneas's wanderings.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: Aeneas is Dido's princely guest and is seated beside her at the feast. His gifts are admired, and Cupid takes his form and face; through Cupid's work, Dido's thoughts become filled with Aeneas.

l: the Trojans, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: The Trojan people attend Dido's feast with the Tyrian guests. They admire the Trojan gifts and the beautiful boy, and they echo the Tyrians' applause for Iopas's song.

l: Tyrians, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: The Tyrian people are admitted to the feast and recline on the painted couches. They admire the Trojan gifts and Cupid in disguise, praise Iopas's song with loud shouts, and join in the celebration of the proposed peace.

l: Tyre, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: Tyre is represented by its lords and royal line at the feast. Dido invokes the Tyrian line when she prays that it may remain in lasting concord with the Trojan line.

l: Trojans and Tyrians' peace, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: Dido calls upon hospitable Jove, Bacchus, and Juno to bless the hour and establish lasting concord between the Trojan and Tyrian lines. She asks the lords of Tyre to make vows with her to ratify the peace.

l: the feast, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: The feast includes bread, water for washing, incense, dishes, wine, golden bowls, and entertainment. After the meal, Dido offers prayers and wine, Bitias drains a large goblet, and Iopas sings while the guests celebrate.

l: the Trojan War, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: Dido asks Aeneas to explain the Trojan War, including the Grecian stratagems, the betrayal of the town, and the fatal outcome of the long conflict. She has already questioned him about Priam, Hector, Memnon, Diomede, and Achilles.

l: Aeneas's flight and wanderings, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: Dido asks Aeneas to describe his flight, wanderings, and woes after the war. She notes that his men have been distressed and his navy tossed on every sea and coast while seven years have passed.

l: the Greeks, The Aeneid, Cupid meantime assum’d his form and face,
s: The Grecians are associated with the stratagems that Dido wants Aeneas to recount. Their actions are connected with the betrayal and fall of the town after the long war.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: Aeneas recounts to the queen how Troy was destroyed after the Greeks, weary of the ten-year siege, used Sinon and the wooden horse to deceive the Trojans. Laocoon warns that the horse conceals Greek soldiers, but the Trojans interpret the appearance of two serpents as proof that Minerva favors admitting it. The Greeks hide their fleet at Tenedos, return by night, and release the warriors concealed inside the horse. The Greek soldiers then kill the sentries, open Troy’s gates, and begin the sack of the city.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: Aeneas relates the destruction of Troy and the events of its final night. He describes what he witnessed and experienced as the Greeks deceived the Trojans with Sinon and the wooden horse.

l: Troy, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: Troy is deceived into admitting the wooden horse after Sinon persuades the Trojans that it will secure their city. Once night falls, Greek soldiers emerge from the horse, open the gates, and begin invading the city.

l: the Trojans, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The Trojans celebrate the Greeks’ apparent departure and debate what to do with the wooden horse. They believe Sinon’s false account and interpret the serpents’ attack on Laocoon as a sign that the horse should be brought inside Troy.

l: the Greeks, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The Greeks construct the wooden horse, conceal selected soldiers inside it, and hide their fleet at Tenedos. They later return under cover of night, release the hidden warriors, and attack Troy while its people sleep.

l: the Trojan War, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The Trojan War has lasted ten years when the Greeks grow weary of the unsuccessful siege. They resort to deception rather than direct assault to achieve victory.

l: the fall of Troy, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The fall of Troy is brought about by the Greeks’ deception, Sinon’s false story, and the Trojans’ decision to admit the wooden horse. The fall begins when the hidden Greeks open the city gates at night.

l: the Trojan horse, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The wooden horse is a huge fabric built by the Greeks with Minerva’s aid and loaded with concealed soldiers. The Trojans haul it into the city despite Laocoon’s warning, after which it becomes the means of their destruction.

l: Sinon, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: Sinon allows himself to be captured and falsely claims that the Greeks intended to sacrifice him before fleeing. He tells the Trojans that the wooden horse was built to reconcile Minerva and that Troy will be destroyed if it is not admitted.

l: Laocoon, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: Laocoon warns the Trojans that the wooden horse contains Greek soldiers or is a weapon intended to destroy the city. While sacrificing a steer, he and his children are attacked and killed by two serpents, leading the Trojans to believe that Minerva punished him.

l: Minerva, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: Minerva is said to have aided the Greeks in constructing the wooden horse. Sinon claims that the Greeks lost her favor after Diomede and Ulysses stole her image, and the Trojans believe that the serpents’ attack on Laocoon shows that she supports admitting the horse.

l: Ulysses, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: Ulysses is presented as a master of deceit who helped accuse Palamedes and later used the Greeks’ fear to arrange Sinon’s supposed sacrifice. He is among the Greek warriors who descend from the wooden horse and invade Troy.

l: Tenedos, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: Tenedos is an island lying in sight of Troy. The Greek fleet hides there so that the Trojans believe the Greeks have sailed away, then returns to Troy during the night.

l: the Greek fleet, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The Greek fleet is concealed at Tenedos after the Trojans mistake its absence for a departure. It later sails back toward Troy under cover of night, guided by the light of the imperial galley.

l: the two serpents, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The two serpents emerge from the sea and swim toward the shore, where they coil around Laocoon’s children and then around Laocoon himself. After killing them, the serpents retreat to Minerva’s tower and lie beneath her protection.

l: the gods, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The gods are invoked throughout the deception and destruction of Troy. Sinon claims that divine signs and religious commands required the Greeks to build the horse, while Aeneas says that Heaven had designed Troy’s fall.

l: Fate, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: Fate is said to compel the Greeks’ actions and to determine the destruction of Troy. Aeneas states that Troy might have survived if Heaven had not destined its fall and the Trojans had not been fated to blindness.

l: the Greeks’ escape from Troy, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The Greeks’ apparent escape from Troy is a deception rather than a true departure. Their fleet hides at Tenedos while the soldiers remain concealed inside the wooden horse, then they return and attack the city.

l: the sack of Troy, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The sack of Troy begins after the Greek soldiers emerge from the wooden horse and open the gates. They first kill the few Trojans who are awake and then admit the rest of the Greek forces.

l: Trojan War, The Aeneid, BOOK II
s: The siege has continued for ten years and has exhausted the Greeks. Unable to win through prolonged warfare, they use the wooden horse and Sinon’s deception to enter Troy.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Aeneas describes how Hector’s ghost warned him that Troy was doomed and charged him to escape with the Trojan gods. He recounts joining Pantheus, Coroebus, and other Trojans in a night battle against the Greeks, briefly using captured Greek arms before the disguise failed. The Greeks overrun the Trojan palace, kill its defenders, and slaughter Priam after Pyrrhus pursues and kills Polites. The account presents the fall and sack of Troy as the fulfillment of divine fate.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Aeneas sees Hector’s ghost, receives the Trojan gods from him, and is warned to escape Troy with them. He joins the defense of the city during the Greek assault, fights with the Trojans, and witnesses the destruction of the palace and the death of Priam.

l: Hector, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Hector appears to Aeneas as a bloody, tearful ghost bearing the wounds inflicted when Pelides killed him and dragged him behind Thessalian coursers. He warns Aeneas that Troy will fall and gives him the Trojan gods, telling him to establish walls elsewhere.

l: Priam, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Priam arms himself despite his age when the Greeks enter his palace. After Pyrrhus kills Polites before him, Priam condemns Pyrrhus and is killed by him on the sacred altar.

l: Cassandra, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Cassandra is dragged by her hair from Minerva’s shrine despite her sacred protections. Coroebus attacks her captors, but the Trojans who follow him are mistaken for Greeks and attacked by their own allies.

l: Coroebus, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Coroebus joins Aeneas and the other Trojans in the defense of Troy, motivated by his love for Cassandra. He proposes that the Trojans wear captured Greek arms, but he is later killed by Peneleus at Pallas’ altar while trying to rescue Cassandra.

l: Pantheus, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Pantheus, Apollo’s priest, escapes the Greek swords and fire with sacred relics and his grandson. He tells Aeneas that Troy is lost, the Greeks have entered through the horse, and the Trojan defenders cannot prevail.

l: Pyrrhus, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Pyrrhus leads the assault on the Trojan palace, breaks through its doors, kills its guards and defenders, and fills the apartments with Greeks. He pursues and kills Polites, then drags Priam to the altar and kills him.

l: household gods, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Hector brings the venerable statues of the Trojan gods, ancient Vesta, the wreaths, and relics of the immortal fire to Aeneas. Their temples are defiled and their abodes abandoned during the Greek assault.

l: the Greeks, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: The Greeks secretly enter Troy through the Trojan horse and attack the city from within and without. They fight the Trojans through the streets, temples, and palace, kill Cassandra’s defenders, and seize the royal household and its treasures.

l: the Trojans, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: The Trojans awaken to the Greek attack, gather under Aeneas, and fight through the night despite having little hope of victory. They briefly defeat Greek parties by using captured armor, but are eventually overwhelmed and killed or driven back.

l: the Trojan royal family, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: The Trojan royal family is trapped in the palace as Pyrrhus and the Greeks break through its doors. Polites is killed before Priam, Priam is slain at the altar, and the palace’s royal rooms, women, and treasures are exposed to the attackers.

l: Troy, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Troy is described as nodding and tottering toward destruction, with its streets, temples, and palaces consumed by fire and battle. Its state is transferred to Greek hands, and its surviving future is entrusted to Aeneas.

l: Ilium, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Ilium is declared to be no more and reduced to the status of a town. Its fire, slaughter, and fall form part of the destruction witnessed during the night attack.

l: the Trojan palace, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: The palace is initially set apart from the streets by a surrounding wood, but its location does not protect it from the assault. The Greeks breach its doors, enter its halls and apartments, and kill its defenders while the royal household seeks shelter.

l: the Trojan horse, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: The Trojan horse conceals armed Greek forces in its hollow interior. When the attack begins, those forces emerge inside the gates and join the Greeks pressing in from outside.

l: the Trojan War, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: The war is recalled through Hector’s former triumphs and the wounds he received for his country. Its final night brings the Greek assault, the collapse of Trojan defenses, and the death of Priam and many others.

l: the fall of Troy, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: The fall of Troy begins with the Greeks possessing the walls, setting fires, and emerging from the horse. The city’s defenders fight with desperation, but the Greeks destroy its temples and palace and take control.

l: the Greek assault on Troy, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: The Greek assault combines fire inside the city, forces emerging from the horse, attacks at the gates, and fighting through the streets. The assault reaches the Trojan palace, where Pyrrhus leads the breach and the killing.

l: the slaughter of the night, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: The night is filled with funerals, fires, tumults, and confused fighting in which both Trojans and Greeks die. Androgeos and his band are ambushed, Coroebus and other Trojans are killed, and many defenders perish in the fighting around the palace.

l: Fate, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: Pantheus says that the appointed hour has come and that Jove’s irrevocable doom transfers the Trojan state to Greek hands. Aeneas also concludes that courage cannot prevail when heaven’s powers refuse their aid.

l: the sack of Troy, The Aeneid, “’Twas in the dead of night, when sleep repairs
s: The Greeks enter and possess the spaces left by the fire, including the royal palace and its treasures. They kill defenders, violate temples, seize the royal spoils, and leave Priam’s body abandoned on the shore.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Aeneas sees Helen hiding in Vesta’s temple and nearly kills her, but Venus appears and reveals that the gods, not Helen and Paris, are destroying Troy. Aeneas returns to Anchises, who first refuses to flee but changes his mind after omens involving Ascanius and a celestial sign. Aeneas carries Anchises, leads Ascanius, and attempts to escape with Creusa, but loses her during the flight. Creusa appears as a ghost and tells Aeneas that fate has decreed a long journey to Latium, where he will found a new kingdom.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Aeneas sees Helen in Vesta’s temple and resolves to punish her, but Venus intervenes and commands him to abandon this fruitless vengeance. He returns to Anchises, prepares the household’s escape, carries his father, leads Ascanius, and tries to guide Creusa through the burning city. After losing Creusa, he searches for her throughout Troy and finally sees her ghost, who tells him to continue toward Latium.

l: Anchises, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Anchises initially refuses to leave Troy, choosing death and burial among its ruins rather than exile and old age. After witnessing the omen of flame around Ascanius and a celestial sign from Jupiter, he accepts that the gods command him to flee. Aeneas carries him from the burning city.

l: Creusa, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Creusa tries to stop Aeneas from returning to battle and urges him to protect his father, son, and wife. She is lost during the escape from Troy and later appears to Aeneas as a ghost. She tells him that the gods have decreed a long journey and that he will reach Latium, where he will find a kingdom and a royal bride.

l: Ascanius, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Ascanius escapes Troy with Aeneas and Creusa. A lambent flame appears around his head, and a subsequent thunderous celestial sign confirms the omen. Aeneas leads him by the hand during the flight.

l: Venus, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Venus appears before Aeneas in heavenly brightness and restrains him from attacking Helen. She reveals the divine forces destroying Troy, including Neptune, Juno, Pallas, and Jupiter, and commands Aeneas to return to Anchises, Creusa, and Ascanius.

l: Helen, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Helen hides alone and muffled in the porch of Vesta’s temple while Troy burns. Aeneas recognizes her and considers killing her, but Venus tells him that Helen and Paris are not responsible for the destruction, which was brought about by the gods.

l: the Greeks, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: The Grecian forces attack and occupy Troy while its buildings burn and collapse. They gather Trojan wealth at Juno’s church, guard captive youths and matrons, and prevent any hope of late relief.

l: the Trojans, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: The Trojan people suffer the destruction of their city, with many killed, despairing, or fleeing. A surviving group of men, women, young, and old gathers with arms and treasure, willing to follow Aeneas through the dangers of sea and land.

l: the gods, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: The gods bring about Troy’s destruction and intervene in the battle. Neptune shakes the foundations, Juno urges on the Grecian forces, Pallas occupies a tower, and Jupiter gives courage to the enemy. The gods also provide omens and direct Aeneas’s escape.

l: Troy, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Troy is consumed by fire, breached by the Grecian forces, and torn from its foundations. Its palaces, houses, temples, walls, and treasures are destroyed or seized, and Aeneas finally abandons the city with the remaining Trojan exiles.

l: Ida, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Ida is the grove toward which the celestial sign travels and disappears. Anchises had intended to take refuge there before deciding to flee with Aeneas.

l: Latium, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Latium is identified by Creusa’s ghost as the destination decreed for Aeneas after many years of wandering by land and sea. There he will find a quiet kingdom and a royal bride, and the Trojan line will be restored.

l: the destruction of Troy, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: The destruction of Troy is presented as the work of the gods rather than the fault of Helen and Paris. Neptune, Juno, Pallas, and Jupiter actively contribute to the city’s ruin while fire and enemy forces overwhelm it.

l: the fall of Troy, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: The fall of Troy leaves its people dead, captive, or in flight. Aeneas witnesses the city’s collapse, abandons hopes of defending it, and leads the surviving Trojan group away.

l: the sack of Troy, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: The flight from Troy begins after Anchises accepts the divine omens. Aeneas carries Anchises, leads Ascanius, and follows Creusa through dark and winding paths, but Creusa is lost before the survivors reach their meeting place.

l: the fire of Troy, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: The fire of Troy spreads through the city as winds drive flames and sparks across the roofs. It consumes buildings, illuminates the destruction, and forces Aeneas and his household to escape.

l: Creusa’s death, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Creusa is lost during the escape and never returns to the survivors. Her ghost tells Aeneas that the gods have determined her fate and that she will not follow him to Latium.

l: Fate, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Fate requires Aeneas to abandon the defense of Troy and undertake a long journey over land and sea. Creusa’s ghost declares that fate will bring him to Latium, where he will establish a kingdom and restore the Trojan line.

l: the omens concerning Ascanius, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: A lambent flame appears around Ascanius’s head without harming him. Soon afterward, thunder sounds and a streaming light crosses the sky toward Ida; Anchises interprets these signs as divine confirmation that the family should flee.

l: the Trojan household gods, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: Aeneas orders the Trojan household gods and sacred relics to be carried to the ruined temple of Ceres. He refuses to carry them himself while still polluted by bloodshed and intends to cleanse himself in a living stream.

l: the Trojan exile, The Aeneid, “Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood
s: The Trojan exile consists of survivors gathered at Ceres’s deserted seat, including men, matrons, young people, and old people. They possess arms and treasure and are prepared to follow Aeneas through the dangers of sea and land.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Aeneas recounts how he and the Trojan survivors leave the fallen Troy, build a fleet near Ida, and settle first in Thrace, where he discovers that Polydore was murdered and buried beneath a bleeding myrtle. They sail to Delos, receive Apollo’s oracle, and mistakenly interpret it as directing them to Crete, but the household gods reveal in a dream that their true destination is Hesperia, or Italy. After abandoning Crete, Aeneas’s fleet is scattered by a storm and reaches the Strophades, where the Harpies attack them and Celaeno prophesies that famine will precede their settlement. Aeneas then visits several shores, including Epirus and Chaonia, and meets Andromache and Helenus at Buthrotus before asking Helenus for further guidance toward Italy.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Aeneas leads the Trojan survivors from the ruins of Troy and recounts their voyage. He settles briefly in Thrace and Crete, learns through the household gods that Italy is their true destination, encounters the Harpies, and visits Helenus and Andromache at Buthrotus.

l: Anchises, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Anchises leads the Trojans to sea, advises them after the discovery of Polydore’s murder, and interprets Apollo’s oracle as directing them to Crete. After the household gods correct this interpretation, he recognizes the connection between the prophecy of Cassandra and the Trojans’ future in Italy.

l: Polydore, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Polydore reveals that he was sent from Troy to Thrace for safety but was murdered by the faithless Thracian ruler for his gold. His buried body becomes the source of the blood that flows from the wounded myrtle.

l: Helenus, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Helenus rules at Buthrotus in Chaonia and is described as having revived the Trojan name in Greece. He receives Aeneas and his companions, and Aeneas asks him for prophetic guidance about the dangers and route to Italy.

l: Andromache, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Andromache lives at Buthrotus with Helenus after being given to him by Pyrrhus. She mourns her former husband Hector, recognizes Aeneas, and asks about Ascanius and the fate of his mother.

l: Celaeno, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Celaeno, identified as the messenger of Fate and the queen of the Furies, remains after the Harpies retreat. She warns Aeneas that his people will reach Italy but will suffer severe famine before building their promised walls.

l: Harpies, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: The Harpies inhabit the Strophades and defile the Trojans’ meals by snatching their food and leaving filth behind. The Trojans try to fight them, but the Harpies’ bodies resist weapons and they escape.

l: the Trojans, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: The Trojans flee the destroyed Troy with Aeneas, Anchises, Ascanius, and their gods. They build settlements in Thrace and Crete, endure plague and storms, confront the Harpies, and continue toward Italy.

l: the ships, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Aeneas’s fleet is built from timber near Antandros and Ida. It sails from Thrace to Delos and Crete, is scattered by a storm after leaving Crete, and later reaches the Strophades, Leucate, Epirus, and Chaonia.

l: household gods, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: The household gods travel with Aeneas from the burning Troy and appear to him in a dream. They explain that Crete is not his destined home and instruct him to search for Hesperia, or Italy.

l: Troy, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Troy is overthrown, Priam’s throne is destroyed, and Ilium’s towers are burned after the Greeks conquer the city. Its surviving people leave with Aeneas, carrying their gods and seeking a new home.

l: Thrace, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Thrace is the first foreign land where Aeneas settles after leaving Troy. Although it was once friendly with Troy, it becomes an accursed shore when Aeneas discovers Polydore’s murdered body there.

l: Delos, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Aeneas’s fleet reaches Delos after leaving Thrace and is welcomed by Anius, its priest and king. At Apollo’s temple, Aeneas asks where the Trojan survivors should establish their permanent home.

l: Crete, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Crete is mistakenly identified by Anchises as the land promised by Apollo’s oracle because the Trojans trace their ancestry to it. Aeneas establishes Pergamus there, but plague and crop failure force the Trojans to leave after the household gods reveal that Crete is not their destined abode.

l: Hesperia, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Hesperia is named by the household gods as a fruitful land with bold inhabitants and is identified with Italy. They say that Jasius and Dardanus were born there and that the Trojans must return to it.

l: Strophades, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: The Strophades are islands in the Ionian Sea and the home of the Harpies. Aeneas lands there, but the Harpies repeatedly ruin the Trojans’ meals and Celaeno delivers her prophecy of famine.

l: Epirus, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Aeneas’s fleet sails along the rocky coast of Epirus after leaving Leucate. It then turns toward Chaonia and the port of Buthrotus.

l: Chaonia, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Chaonia is the region where Helenus rules after succeeding Pyrrhus and where Buthrotus is located. Helenus names the region and its rising walls after Chaon and Pergamus.

l: Buthrotus, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Buthrotus is the port and city where Aeneas meets Helenus and Andromache. Its landscape resembles Troy, with a stream called Xanthus, a Scaean gate, and a city described as a smaller image of Troy.

l: Apollo’s oracle, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Apollo’s oracle tells the Trojan survivors to seek the mother earth from which their ancestors came and promises that the Aeneian house will rule widely. Anchises first interprets the answer as referring to Crete, but the household gods later reveal that it refers to Italy.

l: Polydore’s murder, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Polydore’s murder occurs in Thrace when its ruler kills the Trojan prince for the gold entrusted to him. The Trojans leave the polluted shore only after performing funeral rites and building a tomb and altars for Polydore.

l: the fall of Troy, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: The fall of Troy begins the Trojans’ wandering. After the Greeks take the city and burn Ilium, Aeneas leads the survivors away with Anchises, Ascanius, and their gods.

l: settlement in Crete, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: During the settlement in Crete, Aeneas names a rising town Pergamus, divides land, gives laws, and promotes marriages. The settlement fails when pestilential heat, disease, insects, and blighted crops afflict the people.

l: Cretan plague, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: The Cretan plague corrupts the air, withers the grass and grain, harms the animals, and causes many of Aeneas’s men to die or suffer fever. It leads Anchises to send Aeneas back to Delos to seek further divine guidance.

l: the dream of the household gods, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: In the dream of the household gods, the Trojan gods appear to Aeneas in the moonlight and explain that they have followed and protected him. They correct the mistaken interpretation of Apollo’s oracle and direct him to search for Italy.

l: the Harpies’ curse, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: The Harpies’ curse states that the Trojans will reach the Italian shores but will suffer fierce famine before building their promised walls. Celaeno says the famine is imposed because the Trojans attacked the Harpies and drove them from their home.

l: Anchises’s death, The Aeneid, BOOK III
s: Anchises’s death does not occur in this unit. He remains alive while the fleet leaves Crete, reaches the Strophades, and continues through Leucate and Epirus to Buthrotus.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Aeneas recounts to the queen how Helenus prophesied the dangers and route of the Trojan voyage, including the sow omen, the straits, Scylla, Charybdis, Cumae, and the Sibyl. Helenus and Andromache provide gifts and advice before Aeneas, Anchises, Ascanius, and the Trojans depart from Epirus and sail along Sicily and Italy. On Cyclopian shores, Achaemenides is rescued after being abandoned in Polyphemus’s cave, and the Trojans escape the Cyclopes. Aeneas finally reaches Drepanum, where Anchises dies after their many hardships.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Aeneas consults Helenus, receives instructions for reaching Italy, and continues the Trojan voyage with Anchises, Ascanius, and the Trojans. He rescues Achaemenides from the Cyclopian shores and recounts his wanderings to the queen.

l: Anchises, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Anchises receives gifts and recruits from Helenus and Andromache before departing. He interprets the omen of the four white steeds, identifies Charybdis, offers prayers during the voyage, and dies at Drepanum after enduring many hardships.

l: Helenus, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Helenus gives Aeneas a prophecy about the route to Italy, the sow omen, hostile shores, Scylla and Charybdis, Juno, and the Sibyl at Cumae. He also supplies the Trojans with treasure, arms, ships' crews, pilots, horses, and other warlike stores.

l: Andromache, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Andromache gives Ascanius a robe, a Phrygian vest, and other gifts. She says that Ascanius reminds her of her lost Astyanax and mourns that Astyanax did not live to the same age.

l: Ascanius, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Ascanius receives gifts from Andromache, including a robe and a Phrygian vest, because his features and form remind her of Astyanax.

l: Achaemenides, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Achaemenides, a Greek from Ithaca, says that Ulysses's countrymen abandoned him in the Cyclops’ cave. After three moons of hiding and surviving on roots, herbs, and wild berries, he is rescued by Aeneas and taken aboard the Trojan ships.

l: Polyphemus, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Polyphemus is described as a gigantic, one-eyed shepherd who eats human flesh and drinks blood. After his eye is bored out with a flaming brand, he searches for the departing ships but cannot wade far enough into the sea to reach them.

l: Phoebus, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Phoebus is invoked during the consultation with Helenus and is said to assist the Trojans and guide their fate. Helenus also says that Phoebus designated the farther shore for their settlement.

l: Juno, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Juno is described as hostile and as forbidding Helenus to reveal certain matters. Helenus repeatedly instructs the Trojans to adore Juno, offer gifts, and pray for her aid so that their passage into Italy will be safe.

l: the Trojans, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: The Trojans follow Helenus’s religious and navigational instructions, veil their heads during rites, and sail from Epirus toward Italy. They escape Charybdis and the Cyclopes, rescue Achaemenides, and eventually reach Drepanum.

l: the Greeks, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: The Greeks possess the shores of the region that Helenus warns Aeneas to avoid. Achaemenides is one of the Greeks who fought at Troy and was abandoned by his countrymen in the Cyclops’ cave.

l: the Cyclopes, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: The Cyclopes live on the island around Mount Etna, keeping sheep and herds in caves and on the mountains. They rush to the shore after Polyphemus cries out, but the Trojan fleet escapes them.

l: the gods, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: The gods are invoked throughout the voyage to protect the Trojans, calm winds and waves, and grant them a favorable passage. Helenus says that the gods have preserved Anchises and will favor Aeneas's future settlement.

l: Italy, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Italy is the promised destination of the Trojan voyage, though Helenus warns that it lies farther away than Aeneas expects. The Trojans first see its hills and plains from the sea, but continue along the coast after landing briefly.

l: Sicily, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: The Trojans must cruise along Sicilian shores before reaching Italy. They pass several Sicilian places, encounter Mount Etna and the Cyclopes, and sail around Sicily after avoiding the straits.

l: Troy, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Troy is remembered as the city from which Aeneas and the Trojans derive their origin. Aeneas hopes to establish another Troy in Italy, while Helenus urges him to raise the Trojan state.

l: the straits of Messina, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: The straits are formed where an earthquake broke the land between Italy and Sicily. Helenus warns Aeneas about Scylla and Charybdis there and advises him to keep out to sea rather than approach Scylla.

l: Scylla, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Scylla hides on the right side of the straits and draws sinking vessels into her eddy before dashing them against the rocks. Helenus advises the Trojans to stay away from her and her barking sea-monsters.

l: Charybdis, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Charybdis presides on the left side of the straits, sucking in the tides and spouting them upward. The Trojan ships are driven through violent waves near her, and later Anchises identifies the rocks and orders the fleet to bear out to sea.

l: Cumae, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: At Cumae, Helenus says that Aeneas will find the Sibyl near the black waters of Avernus and the sounding wood. The Sibyl will explain his wars, future suffering, and route to the destined shores.

l: Mount Etna, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Mount Etna is joined to the secure port on the Cyclopian shores and continually emits smoke, embers, flames, rocks, and burning sulphur. Its surrounding caverns echo with the cries of Polyphemus and the Cyclopes.

l: Cyclopian shores, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: The Trojans reach the Cyclopian shores after their passage through dangerous waters and spend a night there. They rescue Achaemenides and depart quickly when Polyphemus and the other Cyclopes appear.

l: Drepanum, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Drepanum receives the weary fleet after its long wanderings and storms. Aeneas says that Anchises dies there, making Drepanum the site of his greatest and final loss.

l: the Cyclops’ cave, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: The Cyclops’ cave is large but dark, with a floor covered by mangled limbs and putrid gore. Polyphemus keeps captives there, and Achaemenides is left behind in it when the Greeks flee.

l: the sow omen, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Helenus says that Aeneas will find a white sow with thirty white young near a wood and a gentle stream. The sow and her offspring will give their name to the city and mark the end of Aeneas's labors and suffering.

l: Helenus’s prophecy, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Helenus’s prophecy describes the distant route to Italy, the dangers of Sicily, the straits, the sow omen, the need to honor Juno, and the consultation with the Sibyl at Cumae. It also directs Aeneas to avoid certain Greek-held shores and predicts the establishment of the Trojan state.

l: Aeneas’s voyage, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: The Trojan voyage proceeds from Helenus’s court through the waters around Sicily and toward Italy. The fleet faces storms, Charybdis, Mount Etna, the Cyclopes, and the loss of Anchises before Aeneas completes this part of his account.

l: the blinding of Polyphemus, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Ulysses and his companions blind Polyphemus by driving a flaming brand into his single eye while he is asleep. The act avenges the Greeks whom Polyphemus killed and enables their escape from the cave.

l: the Trojan state, The Aeneid, “The prophet first with sacrifice adores
s: Helenus tells Aeneas to raise the Trojan state by strength of arms. Aeneas also hopes to build a city in Italy and establish lasting concord between the Trojan lines descended from Troy and those settled by Helenus and Andromache.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Dido confesses to Anna that she loves Aeneas, though she remains bound by her vows to the dead Sichaeus. Anna encourages the relationship, and Dido and Aeneas become united in a cave during a storm arranged by Juno, after which Fame spreads reports of their affair. Jupiter sends Mercury to command Aeneas to leave Carthage and fulfill his fate of founding a future empire in Ausonia and Latium for Ascanius and Rome.

l: Dido, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Dido falls deeply in love with Aeneas and tells Anna that his worth, suffering, speech, and appearance have revived feelings like those she had for Sichaeus. She calls her relationship with Aeneas a marriage after their sheltering together in the cave, neglects the construction of Carthage, and is denounced by Fame for abandoning her royal duties and reputation.

l: Anna, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Anna listens to Dido's confession and urges her not to waste her life in grief or remain without a husband and children. She argues that an alliance with Aeneas would strengthen Carthage, and her counsel encourages Dido to pursue the relationship.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Aeneas is admired by Dido for his valor, actions, birth, appearance, and suffering at Troy. He joins the hunt, shelters with Dido in the cave, helps raise Carthage's defenses, and is then rebuked by Mercury for lingering in Libya instead of pursuing the future city assigned to him.

l: Ascanius, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Ascanius leads the Trojan youths during the hunt and eagerly rides through the valley in pursuit of game. Jupiter's command reminds Aeneas that Ascanius is destined to receive the Ausonian scepter and state.

l: Juno, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Juno sees Dido consumed by love and proposes to Venus that Dido and Aeneas be joined, presenting the union as a way to unite their peoples. She arranges for a storm to scatter the hunting party and drive Dido and Aeneas into one cave, where she intends their bridal union to be completed.

l: Venus, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Venus recognizes the hidden purpose behind Juno's proposal but accepts the plan with apparent agreement. She worries that the alliance could divert Trojan power from its destined course to the shores of Libya.

l: Jupiter, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Jupiter hears Hyarbas's prayer and sees Dido and Aeneas absorbed in their love at Carthage. He sends Mercury to order Aeneas to leave Libya and pursue the future empire and fame destined for Ascanius and the Romans.

l: Mercury, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Mercury obeys Jupiter, flies to Carthage, and finds Aeneas raising the city's defenses while wearing Dido's gifts. In his own form, he rebukes Aeneas for building foreign walls and commands him to leave, reminding him of Ascanius's destined inheritance.

l: Fate, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Fate has assigned Aeneas a future city and a martial race in Latian or Ausonian lands. Jupiter's message says that Aeneas must not delay in Libya because Ascanius and Rome's imperial name are owed their promised future by fate.

l: Cupid, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Love seizes Dido after Aeneas's arrival and grows through his words, looks, and story. It causes her to neglect Carthage's works and abandon secrecy, while the text also presents love as a force that overcomes her vows and sense of honor.

l: Fame, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Fame spreads the report of Dido's relationship with Aeneas throughout the Libyan cities and eventually carries it to Hyarbas. She is portrayed as a vast, sleepless power who enlarges rumors, mixes truth with lies, and accuses Dido of abandoning honor and royal responsibility.

l: Carthage, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Carthage is the rising Tyrian city ruled by Dido, surrounded by enemies and still incomplete. Its towers, walls, mounds, and harbor works are neglected while Dido and Aeneas pursue their love, and Jupiter orders Aeneas to leave the city.

l: Troy, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Troy is the fallen city for which Aeneas fought and suffered. Dido admires his brave attempts on behalf of Troy, while Mercury reminds him that he must not forget his own people and their destined future.

l: Rome, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Rome is presented as the future imperial state whose name and immortal fame depend on Aeneas fulfilling his destiny. Mercury tells Aeneas that Ascanius is owed the Ausonian scepter and the state associated with Rome's imperial name.

l: Latium, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Latium is the land where Aeneas is destined to rule a martial race descended from Teucer. Jupiter's message contrasts this promised Latian future with Aeneas's lingering in Libya.

l: Ausonia, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Ausonia is the coast Aeneas must reach instead of remaining with Dido in Carthage. Jupiter's command identifies it as the destination where Aeneas must redeem his lost honor and secure the future promised to his race.

l: Libya, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Libya contains Carthage, where Aeneas remains absorbed in pleasure and construction. Jupiter regards Aeneas's stay there as a delay that threatens the fulfillment of his destiny.

l: Dido and Aeneas's cave union, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: During the storm, Dido and Aeneas take shelter together in one cave, where the earth, fires, Juno, and the nymphs are described as witnessing their love. From this ill-omened union arise debate, death, and succeeding woes, and Dido later calls it a marriage.

l: the hunt, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Dido, Aeneas, Ascanius, and the Tyrian and Trojan company go hunting in the hills with hounds, horses, nets, and weapons. The hunt is arranged as part of Juno's plan to separate the party and bring Dido and Aeneas into the same cave.

l: the storm, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Juno sends a violent storm of hail, thunder, lightning, and rain over the hunting party. The storm disperses the company and drives Dido and Aeneas into a common cavern.

l: the divine command to leave Carthage, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: Jupiter's command requires Aeneas to leave Carthage and stop wasting his days in pleasure and delay. Through Mercury, Jupiter reminds him that he must pursue the city and martial race promised by fate, as well as Ascanius's future in Ausonia and Rome.

l: Dido’s impending death, The Aeneid, BOOK IV
s: The argument states that when Aeneas cannot be persuaded to remain, Dido contrives her own death, with the book concluding on that event. In the passage itself, her death is foreshadowed by the statement that her cave union leads to debate, death, and succeeding woes.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Aeneas secretly prepares the Trojan fleet to leave the Tyrian court after Jove commands him to seek the promised Latian lands. Dido discovers his plan, confronts him, and pleads with him to stay, but Aeneas says that fate, the gods, and the divine command compel his departure. Dido curses Aeneas and sends Anna to ask for a delay, yet Aeneas remains firm while the Trojans ready their ships. Dido is left overwhelmed by grief and facing death.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Aeneas secretly orders the fleet repaired and the men embarked, intending to leave the Tyrian court. He tells Dido that the Delphian oracle, fate, Jove, and the appearance of the herald of the gods require him to seek the Latian lands. Though he mourns and feels pity and love for Dido, he obeys the will of Jove and keeps his purpose.

l: Dido, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Dido discovers Aeneas’s preparations and confronts him with grief, anger, and accusations of ingratitude and broken faith. She reminds him that she saved him and the Trojans, fed them, took him to her throne and bed, and restored his fleet. She asks first for his continued stay and later only for a short delay, but her pleas fail.

l: Anna, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Anna receives Dido’s request to approach Aeneas and ask him to delay his departure. She carries Dido’s mournful message and adds her own tears, but Aeneas refuses her appeals.

l: Jupiter, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Jove commands Aeneas to leave the Tyrian court and seek the promised Latian lands. His command keeps Aeneas from yielding to Dido’s pleas.

l: the Trojans, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: The Trojans repair and prepare the fleet, gather at the beach, and load the ships for departure. They are compared to ants carrying provisions toward their cells.

l: the gods, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: The gods, through the Delphian oracle and the herald sent from Jove, direct Aeneas toward the Latian lands. Dido accuses the gods of allowing Aeneas’s treachery, but Aeneas says that their command must be obeyed.

l: Carthage, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: The Tyrian court is the land Aeneas prepares to leave. Dido has adorned its Libyan town with walls and towers, while the Trojans’ preparations fill its shore and harbor with activity.

l: Libya, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Libya is the foreign land where Dido, a Tyrian stranger, has adorned a town with walls and towers. Dido says that Aeneas, also of foreign origin, should be able to seek shelter in a foreign place.

l: Troy, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Troy is the place Aeneas says he would choose to revisit and restore if heaven allowed him freedom from fate. He says that even the restoration of Troy and Priam’s reign would not release him from the command to seek the Latian lands.

l: Latium, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Latium is the promised place to which Aeneas is commanded to steer. He says that all his vows are terminated there and that he must pursue its promised kingdom.

l: Trojan fleet, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Aeneas orders the fleet repaired and secretly prepares it for departure. The fleet is soon afloat, with its galleys ready in the harbor, and the Trojans continue loading it.

l: the ships, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: The ships are repaired, fitted out, and prepared for sailing. Their crews gather aboard, bind them with garlands, invoke the sea gods, and prepare to use the wind.

l: the sea, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: The sea is the route Aeneas intends to take toward the Latian lands. Dido says that its waves are less false than Aeneas and prays that they or hidden sands will become sepulchers for his vessels and their perjured lord.

l: the divine command to leave Carthage, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: The divine command comes from Jove through the herald of the gods and directs Aeneas toward the Latian lands. Aeneas presents it as an unavoidable order, and it causes him to reject Dido’s pleas for delay.

l: Aeneas’s departure, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Aeneas’s departure is planned in secret, then becomes evident as the fleet is repaired, loaded, and made ready to sail. Despite Dido’s repeated appeals, he remains resolved to leave and obeys the will of Jove.

l: the relationship between Dido and Aeneas, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Dido says that she and Aeneas have exchanged vows, shared new nuptial pleasures, and that she took him to her throne and bed. Their relationship is broken by Aeneas’s decision to leave, which Dido experiences as betrayal while he treats it as obedience to fate and the gods.

l: Dido’s impending death, The Aeneid, The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear;
s: Dido speaks of being a despairing queen and says that she will die if Aeneas leaves. She asks for only enough delay to prepare her soul for continued grief, while her curses invoke her future death and angry ghost.

l: The Aeneid, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: Dido, devastated by Aeneas’s departure, prepares secret funeral rites and resolves to die. Aeneas, warned by Hermes, orders the Trojans to sail away before dawn, and Dido curses him, his people, and their descendants. Dido kills herself on the funeral pile with Aeneas’s sword, while Anna discovers the deception and tries unsuccessfully to save her. Juno sends Iris to cut Dido’s fatal hair, releasing her soul from her body.

l: Dido, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: Dido is consumed by grief, rage, despair, and love after Aeneas leaves. She deceives Anna about the purpose of the funeral rites, curses Aeneas and the Trojans, and kills herself on the funeral pile.

l: Anna, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: Anna believes Dido’s rites are intended to end her love rather than her life and helps construct the funeral pile. After Dido wounds herself, Anna rushes to her, embraces her, tries to staunch the blood, and laments that Dido has destroyed herself and her city.

l: Aeneas, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: Aeneas sleeps more easily than Dido and prepares the Trojans for an early departure. After Hermes warns him again, he orders the fleet to sail and leaves without knowing that Dido is about to kill herself.

l: Mercury, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: Hermes appears to Aeneas in a dream in the form of a young man and warns him that Dido harbors furious hatred and intends to die. He urges Aeneas to flee before dawn, then disappears into the night.

l: Tyrians, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: Dido imagines that the Tyrians would have attacked and destroyed the Trojan band at their queen’s command. In her dying curse, she orders the Tyrians to maintain perpetual hatred and mortal wars against Aeneas, his people, and their name.

l: the Trojans, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: The Trojans respond quickly to Aeneas’s command, rushing aboard their ships and rowing out to sea. Dido curses them and their descendants, praying that their entrance into the Latian lands will be opposed by war and hardship.

l: Carthage, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: Carthage is described as the new city whose temples and homes might have been consumed by fire during a catastrophe. Dido also recalls that she has raised a lofty city by her own hands.

l: Trojan fleet, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: The Trojan fleet is prepared for departure during the night and sails away before dawn. When Dido sees the ships at sea, she is overcome with fury and despair and wishes to pursue, burn, and destroy them.

l: Dido’s funeral pile, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: Dido’s funeral pile is secretly erected in the court from cloven holms, pines, garlands, cypress, vervain, and yew. It holds Aeneas’s garments, weapons, gifts, image, and the bed associated with their love, and Dido climbs onto it before killing herself.

l: Dido’s sword, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: Dido uses the sword Aeneas left behind to kill herself. She unsheathes it on the funeral pile and strikes herself, driving the weapon deeply into her side.

l: Dido’s magic rites, The Aeneid, The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate,
s: Dido claims that a Massylian priestess can use magic to loosen or fix love, stop torrents, repel stars, summon ghosts, and shake the earth. The rites include altars, invocations of underworld powers, herbs gathered by moonlight, baleful juices, and the blood of a newborn foal, but Dido conceals that they are preparations for her suicide.
